Caño Island lies off Costa Rica's Pacific coast and is known for its biological and archaeological significance. Marine habitats surround the island, with coral formations alongside underwater volcanic rock. Fish and other marine organisms gather in these waters.

Trips to Caño Island feature snorkeling and diving. The boat journey offers views of the island and coastline, while exploring the underwater world reveals another side of the area's natural environment. Caño Island often complements a visit to Corcovado, bringing tropical rainforest and marine ecosystems together in one journey.

Caño Negro protects the wetland landscapes of northern Costa Rica. The Frío River runs through this natural area and provides a route for boat excursions. Exploring from the water lets visitors see the riverbanks and wildlife among the shoreline vegetation without lengthy walks through the forest.

Birds are a particular highlight, including herons and cormorants. Caimans, lizards, and turtles can be seen along the banks and near the water, while monkeys and sloths may be spotted among the trees. Visits to the area are associated with Los Chiles, near the Nicaraguan border. Caño Negro reveals Costa Rica's river and marshland environments.

Capitólio is known in tour programs as the "Sea of Minas." The area is associated with Furnas Lake and journeys through rocky landscapes.

Boat excursions take visitors past canyons and waterfalls. After long stretches on the road, travelers spend a day by the water here, with time to relax and swim as part of their chosen excursion.
